lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Decomposition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking
objectives: Define and apply decomposition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking
Decompose a problem into smaller sub-problems
Identify which details to keep and which to ignore (abstraction)

keywords.def: a way of solving problems using decomposition, abstraction and algorithms
breaking a problem into smaller, manageable parts
removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters
a sequence of steps or rules to solve a problem

starter: Bismillah. Define the term algorithm in one sentence.
Write the steps to make a cup of tea, as an algorithm, in under 6 steps.
Why does a map of the London Underground leave out most of the real geography?

teach.heading: Computational thinking
bullets: Abstraction: focus on the important detail.
teach.note: Introduce the three skills as the toolkit for the whole course; Paper 2 asks you to apply computational thinking to problems. Pose the question: how would you design a prayer-times app? Collect ideas, then organise them.

teach.heading: Decomposition example
bullets: Sub-problem 3: keep score and show result.
teach.note: Show the tree diagram. Benefits: easier to understand, different people can work on each part, parts can be tested separately and reused. A common mistake in exams is to give a generic answer; always relate to the scenario in the question.

teach.heading: Abstraction example
bullets: Tube map: stations and lines only.
teach.note: Ask pupils what a satnav needs and ignores (it needs roads, speed limits; it ignores the colour of buildings). Define abstraction exactly: filtering out details we do not need so we can focus on the problem. Another example is a variable representing a value.

teach.heading: Algorithmic thinking
bullets: Work out the steps in order.
Decide the inputs, processes and outputs.
teach.note: Model an input-process-output table for 'calculate the average of three marks': inputs mark1, mark2, mark3; process add and divide by 3; output the average. Exams often ask you to identify inputs, processes and outputs.

practice: Decompose the problem 'create a program to run a school canteen till' into at least three sub-problems.
A bus route map shows stops and numbers but not the exact bends in the road. Which computational thinking skill is this?
State one benefit of decomposition for a team creating a game.
independent: Decompose the problem of a program that manages a mosque's weekly timetable. Draw a tree diagram with at least three levels.
List the details to keep and details to ignore when abstracting a model of a car park for a ticket machine.
Write an input-process-output table for a program that calculates the cost of a taxi journey from miles and price per mile.
exit: Define abstraction.
Give one reason for using decomposition when writing a large program.
lessons.homework: Choose a real system (such as an online shop). Describe how it could be decomposed and what abstractions it uses. Write 150 words.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a tree diagram template and sentence stems ('This is abstraction because...'). Stretch: evaluate whether a given abstraction has removed too much detail.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Flowcharts
objectives: Use the standard flowchart symbols correctly
Interpret and complete a flowchart for an algorithm
Create a flowchart for a problem with selection and iteration

keywords.def: a diagram showing the steps of an algorithm using standard symbols
oval symbol marking start or end
diamond symbol with two exits, yes and no
rectangle symbol for an action or calculation
parallelogram symbol for data entering or leaving

starter: Bismillah. State the three parts of computational thinking.
Which flowchart symbol is used for a yes/no question?
What is the difference between selection and iteration?

teach.heading: Flowchart symbols
teach.note: Use the Edexcel-style symbols. Remind pupils that arrows show direction and that each diamond must have two labelled exits (Yes/No). Marks are lost for unlabelled decisions.

teach.heading: Selection in a flowchart
teach.note: Draw this step by step. Trace with n = 7 (odd) and n = 10 (even). Ask what MOD does. Link to Y9 learning: remainders. Use the phrase 'follow the arrows' when tracing.

teach.heading: Iteration in a flowchart
bullets: Set total to 0 and count to 1.
Yes: add count to total, add 1 to count, loop back.
teach.note: Show how a loop is made by an arrow going back to a decision. Trace this algorithm: it outputs 15. Ask pupils what it calculates (sum of 1 to 5). A common mistake is forgetting to increase the counter, causing an infinite loop.

teach.heading: Exam technique
bullets: Use a ruler and correct shapes.
teach.note: Teach pupils to check any flowchart they draw using test data. Mention that on Paper 1 they may need to complete missing parts of a flowchart or say what the algorithm does. Use command words: 'complete', 'describe', 'state'.

practice: Which symbol would you use for 'Input the user's age'? (parallelogram)
Trace the sum flowchart. What are the values of count and total at each pass? (count 1,2,3,4,5; total 1,3,6,10,15)
Add the missing labels to a decision diamond which asks 'Is the temperature above 30?'
independent: Draw a flowchart for an algorithm that inputs a mark and outputs 'Pass' if it is 40 or more, otherwise 'Fail'.
Draw a flowchart which asks for numbers repeatedly until the user enters 0, then outputs how many numbers were entered (not counting 0).
Trace your flowchart with test data 5, 8, 2, 0 and write down the final output.
exit: Name the shape used for a decision and explain what must be on its exits.
State the output of the sum flowchart if the limit changes from 5 to 4.
lessons.homework: Draw a flowchart for an algorithm that asks for a password up to 3 times and ends with 'Locked' if all attempts are wrong.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide symbol stencils and partly completed flowcharts. Stretch: draw a flowchart with a nested decision for a ticket price calculator.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Pseudo-code and trace tables
objectives: Read and write algorithms in pseudo-code using sequence, selection and iteration
Complete a trace table for an algorithm
Identify the purpose of an algorithm and find errors

keywords.def: a way of writing algorithms in structured English not tied to a programming language
a table used to record the values of variables as an algorithm runs
a named store whose value can change
a mistake that makes a program run but give the wrong result

starter: Bismillah. Draw the symbol for a decision.
Why is a flowchart useful before coding?
What is the value of 17 MOD 5?

teach.heading: What is pseudo-code?
bullets: No strict syntax, but be clear.
teach.note: Explain that Pearson's papers present algorithms in pseudo-code (and flowcharts) and that you should check the specification's conventions for the exact style; clear, consistent structure is what matters. Show how to write assignments, inputs and outputs. Keep to one style throughout.

teach.heading: Pseudo-code example
teach.note: Walk through the algorithm: i = 1 → total 2; i = 2 → total 6; i = 3 → total 12; i = 4 → total 20. Present the trace table with the columns i and total. Pupils should fill the table as you go and see that the output is 20.

teach.heading: Trace tables
teach.note: Show a second example with selection: SET x TO 12, IF x MOD 2 = 0 THEN OUTPUT 'even' ELSE OUTPUT 'odd'. Teach pupils to record every change and not to skip rows. Common mistake: updating two variables on one row when they change at different steps.

teach.heading: Purpose and errors
bullets: State what it does in one sentence.
Look for off-by-one and wrong operators.
teach.note: Give an algorithm that finds the largest of three numbers with a bug (uses < instead of >). Trace it with 5, 9, 2 to show the wrong result. Explain syntax errors vs logic errors. Discuss how testing with boundary data finds errors.

practice: Trace: SET a TO 3; SET b TO 4; SET c TO a * b; SET a TO c - a; OUTPUT a. (a = 9)
State the purpose: SET count TO 0; FOR i FROM 1 TO 10; IF i MOD 2 = 0 THEN SET count TO count + 1; OUTPUT count. (counts even numbers from 1 to 10, outputs 5)
Spot the error: an algorithm meant to output the highest of two numbers outputs the lower one.
independent: Complete a trace table for: SET n TO 5; SET f TO 1; WHILE n > 1; SET f TO f * n; SET n TO n - 1; END WHILE; OUTPUT f. (output 120)
Write pseudo-code that inputs 3 numbers and outputs the largest.
Write pseudo-code to output the total of the numbers 1 to 100, and state the expected answer (5050).
exit: What is the purpose of a trace table?
State the output of: SET x TO 2; FOR i FROM 1 TO 3; SET x TO x * 2; OUTPUT x. (16)
lessons.homework: Write pseudo-code for a program which asks for 5 test marks and outputs the average. Trace it with 60, 70, 80, 90, 100.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide trace table templates and pre-filled first rows; use colour to track variables. Stretch: find and correct two errors in an unfamiliar pseudo-code algorithm.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Searching algorithms: linear and binary search
objectives: Describe and carry out a linear search
Describe and carry out a binary search on a sorted list
Compare the two searches and choose the right one

keywords.def: checks each item in turn from the start until the target is found or the list ends
repeatedly checks the middle item of a sorted list and halves the search area
arranged in order, such as lowest to highest
how few steps or how little time or memory an algorithm needs

starter: Bismillah. Trace: SET x TO 3; SET x TO x + 4; OUTPUT x.
How do you look up a name in a printed phone book?
What does 'sorted' mean for a list of numbers?

teach.heading: Linear search
bullets: Compare each item with the target.
Stop when found or at the end.
teach.note: Search [14, 9, 22, 5, 17] for 22: compare 14, 9, 22 found at the third position (3 comparisons). Search for 30: all 5 compared, not found. Note it works on any list, sorted or not.

teach.heading: Binary search idea
bullets: Target smaller? Discard the right half.
Target bigger? Discard the left half.
teach.note: Link to guessing a number between 1 and 100 and being told higher or lower. State the rule for a list with an even number of items: pick a consistent middle (e.g. the lower middle) and follow it, which is acceptable as long as it is clear. Misconception: binary search works on unsorted lists; it does not.

teach.heading: Worked example
teach.note: Draw the list as boxes and cross out the discarded half each time. Count comparisons: 3 for binary against 6 for linear. Show how with 1,000,000 items binary search needs about 20 comparisons at most. State that this is why sorted data is valuable.

teach.heading: Choosing a search
teach.note: Pose a scenario: a list of 10 names unsorted versus 1 million sorted student IDs. Ask which search to choose and why. Exam answers should compare efficiency and the requirement for sorted data.

practice: Linear search for 5 in [8, 3, 5, 9]. How many comparisons? (3)
Why can't you use binary search on [9, 2, 7, 4]? (not sorted)
Binary search for 12 in [2, 5, 9, 12, 15, 20, 31]. Which item is checked first? (12, the middle item, found immediately)
independent: Carry out a linear search for 40 in [52, 12, 40, 8, 27] and record each comparison.
Carry out a binary search for 8 in [3, 8, 12, 15, 21, 27, 34, 40, 52] showing low, high and middle each time.
Write a paragraph comparing linear and binary search, with one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
exit: State one requirement for using binary search.
Which search is usually faster on a large sorted list, and why?
lessons.homework: Write pseudo-code for a linear search that outputs the position of a target in a list or 'not found'. Test with two lists.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide cards to physically cross out halves; show each step in colour. Stretch: work out the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs for 31 items (5).

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Sorting algorithms: bubble sort
objectives: Describe how a bubble sort works
Carry out a bubble sort on a list, showing each pass
Explain when the algorithm can stop

keywords.def: arrange data in order
compares neighbouring items and swaps them if out of order, repeating passes
one complete run through the list
exchange the positions of two items

starter: Bismillah. Name the two searches we studied and state when binary search can be used.
Put these in order: 7, 2, 9, 4.
Explain how you physically sorted a hand of cards when you last played a card game.

teach.heading: Why sort?
bullets: Sorted data is easier to search.
Used in contacts, scores and files.
teach.note: Ask for examples of sorted data in apps (alphabetical contacts, leaderboards). Explain we need precise instructions for a computer to sort.

teach.heading: How bubble sort works
bullets: Swap if they are in the wrong order.
Move along one place and repeat.
teach.note: Demonstrate with 5 pupils holding number cards or with number cards on screen. Largest values 'bubble' to the end. After pass 1 the largest item is in its final position.

teach.heading: Worked example
teach.note: Show every comparison in pass 1: compare 5, 3 swap giving 3 5 8 1; compare 5, 8 no swap; compare 8, 1 swap giving 3 5 1 8. Count swaps per pass. A common mistake is to stop after pass 3 without a final pass proving no swaps are needed (but accept if all in place and explain).

teach.heading: Strengths and weaknesses
bullets: Needs many passes on big lists.
teach.note: Compare: for n items bubble sort may need around n × n comparisons. Do not require formulas at GCSE, but pupils should state it is inefficient for large lists. Use a flag: if no swaps in a pass, stop early.

practice: Carry out pass 1 of a bubble sort on 4, 2, 7, 1. (2 4 1 7)
How many swaps happen in pass 1 on 3, 2, 1? (2) What is the list after pass 1? (2 1 3)
How does the algorithm know it is finished?
independent: Bubble sort 9, 4, 7, 2, 6, writing the list after each pass and the number of swaps.
Write pseudo-code for one pass of a bubble sort on a list called nums with n items.
Explain two weaknesses of bubble sort for a list of one million items.
exit: State what happens in a bubble sort when two neighbouring items are in the wrong order.
After one pass of 6, 5, 1, 4 what is the list? (5 1 4 6)
lessons.homework: Bubble sort the list 12, 5, 9, 1, 8 and show every pass. Explain how you know when to stop.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use physical number cards and highlighters to mark the pair being compared. Stretch: describe how a flag variable could stop the sort early.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Sorting algorithms: merge sort and comparing sorts
objectives: Describe how a merge sort splits and merges lists
Carry out a merge sort on a list of 8 items
Compare bubble sort and merge sort

keywords.def: splits a list into single items, then merges them back in order
solving a problem by splitting it into smaller problems
combine two sorted lists into one sorted list
storage used while the algorithm is running

starter: Bismillah. After one pass of bubble sort on 4, 3, 2, 1 what is the list? (3 2 1 4)
Why does bubble sort slow down on large lists?
How would you sort a pile of 100 exam papers with the help of 3 friends?

teach.heading: Split then merge
bullets: Keep splitting the list in half.
Stop at lists of one item.
Merge pairs of lists back in order.
teach.note: Introduce merge sort as a divide and conquer algorithm and link to decomposition. A list of one item is already sorted. Show the stages with arrows.

teach.heading: Splitting
teach.note: Draw the split tree. Emphasise that no sorting happens while splitting; it all happens during merging. Common mistake: trying to sort during the split stage.

teach.heading: Merging
bullets: Compare the first items of each list.
Move the smaller one to the new list.
Repeat until both lists are used.
teach.note: Merge 6 and 2 to get 2 6; 8 and 4 to get 4 8; 3 and 7 to get 3 7; 1 and 5 to get 1 5. Then merge 2 6 with 4 8: compare 2 and 4, take 2; compare 6 and 4, take 4; compare 6 and 8, take 6; then 8: result 2 4 6 8. Merge 3 7 with 1 5: 1 3 5 7. Final merge gives 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8.

teach.heading: Bubble vs merge
bullets: Merge sort is faster on large lists.
Bubble sort is simpler to write.
teach.note: Give exam-style comparison language: merge sort is more efficient (fewer comparisons) for large data sets but uses more memory because it creates new lists; bubble sort is simple but slow. Ask pupils to decide for a list of 10 items versus 10 million.

practice: Merge the sorted lists 2 5 9 and 1 6 8. (1 2 5 6 8 9)
Split 7 3 9 1 5 2 into halves and halves again. (7 3 9 | 1 5 2 then 7 | 3 9 | 1 | 5 2 and so on)
State one advantage and one disadvantage of merge sort.
independent: Merge sort 9, 3, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6, 4, showing the split and merge stages in a diagram.
Compare bubble sort and merge sort in a table with three rows: how it works, speed on large lists, memory use.
Write a 4-mark answer: 'Explain which sorting algorithm would be better for sorting 1 million customer records.'
exit: What does a merge sort do first?
Give one reason merge sort needs more memory than bubble sort.
lessons.homework: Merge sort the list 14, 3, 9, 20, 1, 7 and show your working. Then explain why merge sort is a divide and conquer algorithm.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a split-and-merge template with boxes; use number cards. Stretch: count the comparisons used in your merge sort and compare with a bubble sort of the same list.

lessons.title: First Python programs: variables, data types, input and output
lessons.bigQuestion: If a program asks your age and you type 14, does the computer know 14 is a number?
objectives: To understand how variables, data types, input and output work in a simple Python program
successCriteria: All: write a program that inputs a name and outputs a greeting
Most: convert input to int or float before calculating
Some: explain why input() always returns a string
lessons.smsc: Moral: clear, honest code others can read and trust

keywords.def: a named location that stores data
the kind of data: int, float, str, bool
data entered into a program
converting from one data type to another

hook.text: If a program asks your age and you type 14, does the computer know 14 is a number?
hook.a: No: input() gives text (a string); we must convert it with int() to calculate with it.

starter.q: A decision in a flowchart is a ...

teach.heading: Model program
teach.note: Trace it together line by line.

code.text:
name = input('Name: ')
age = int(input('Age: '))
next_year = age + 1
print('Salaam', name)
print('Next year you will be', next_year)
code.output:
Name: Yusuf
Age: 14
Salaam Yusuf
Next year you will be 15

teach.heading: Variables
bullets: A named place to store data

misconception.right: input() returns a string: use int(input(...)) before adding

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share results; explain the right answer and the trap in the others.

check.q: What does input() return?
check.why: Always a string; convert with int() or float().

practice.q: Write a program that inputs the price of an item and a quantity, then outputs the total.
practice.a: price = float(input('Price: ')); qty = int(input('Quantity: ')); print('Total', price * qty)
practice.model: I do: price = float(input('Price: ')) because prices have pence; qty = int(input('Quantity: ')); total = price * qty; print('Total:', total).

practice.q: Which converts '3.5' to a number?

independent.q: Pupil PDF task: write a program that inputs minutes and outputs hours and minutes (e.g. 135 → 2 hours 15 minutes). Test with 135, 60 and 59.
independent.a: mins = int(input()); print(mins // 60, 'hours', mins % 60, 'minutes'). 135 → 2 15; 60 → 1 0; 59 → 0 59.
independent.model: The teacher shows // (integer division) and % (modulus): 135 // 60 = 2, 135 % 60 = 15.

independent.q: Extend: add a meaningful comment to each line.
independent.a: Comments with # explaining each step.

independent.q: Stretch: what happens if the user types 'ten'? Why?
independent.a: A runtime error (ValueError): int() cannot convert 'ten'.

exit.q: Which is a Boolean value?
exit.a: True

exit.q: Back to our ponder: If a program asks your age and you type 14, does the computer know 14 is a number?
exit.a: No: input() gives text (a string); we must convert it with int() to calculate with it.

lessons.homework: Write a program that inputs two test marks and outputs the average; bring it next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: printed code with line numbers and a keyword card; pair programming. EAL: glossary of Python keywords. Stretch: extend the program with validation or a function.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Programming 2: data structures, files and subprograms
lessons.title: Lists and arrays: storing and searching many values
lessons.bigQuestion: A teacher records 15 test marks. Would you rather have 15 variables or one list? Why?
objectives: To understand how lists store many values under one name and how to loop through them to search and total
successCriteria: All: create a list and access an item by index
Most: loop through a list to total or find the largest value
Some: implement a linear search returning the position
lessons.smsc: Social: organising data to serve people well

keywords.def: an ordered collection of values under one name
the position of an item, starting at 0
go through each item in turn
check each item in turn until found

hook.text: A teacher records 15 test marks. Would you rather have 15 variables or one list? Why?
hook.a: One list: easier to store, loop through, sort and search.

teach.heading: Lists (arrays) and indexes
teach.note: Index starts at 0 (zero-based).

code.text:
marks = [62, 75, 48, 90]
print(marks[0])
print(marks[3])
print(len(marks))
marks.append(81)
print(marks)

marks = [62, 75, 48, 90]
total = 0
highest = marks[0]
for m in marks:
    total = total + m
    if m > highest:
        highest = m
print(total, highest)

names = ['Ali', 'Huda', 'Musa', 'Safa']
target = input('Find: ')
found = -1
for i in range(len(names)):
    if names[i] == target:
        found = i
print(found)

misconception.right: Lists are zero-based: the first item is marks[0]

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share results; explain the right answer and the trap in the others.

check.q: names = ['Ali', 'Huda', 'Musa']. What is names[2]?
check.why: Index 2 is the third item.

practice.q: Write code to find the average of marks = [62, 75, 48, 90].
practice.a: total = 0; for m in marks: total += m; print(total / len(marks)) → 68.75
practice.model: I do: total = sum by looping: 62 + 75 + 48 + 90 = 275. Average = 275 / len(marks) = 275 / 4 = 68.75.

independent.q: Pupil PDF: a list of 8 daily step counts. Write a program that outputs the total, the highest and how many days were over 8,000.
independent.a: Loop with total, highest, and a counter for values > 8000; answers for the given data on the sheet.
independent.model: The teacher writes the loop header and the counter: count = 0; for s in steps: if s > 8000: count = count + 1

independent.q: Extend: change the linear search to print 'Not found' when found is still -1.
independent.a: if found == -1: print('Not found') else: print(found)

independent.q: Stretch: why is linear search slow on a list of a million names?
independent.a: It may check every item: up to a million comparisons.

exit.q: Lists in Python are ...
exit.a: zero-based

exit.q: Back to our ponder: A teacher records 15 test marks. Would you rather have 15 variables or one list? Why?
exit.a: One list: easier to store, loop through, sort and search.

lessons.homework: Write a list of your five daily prayers' times and print each with a loop.
lessons.send: SEND: printed code with line numbers and a keyword card; pair programming. EAL: glossary of Python keywords. Stretch: extend the program with validation or a function.

lessons.title: Problem solving core: decomposition, abstraction and algorithms
lessons.bigQuestion: How would you explain to a robot how to make a cup of tea? What details could it ignore?
objectives: To understand how decomposition and abstraction turn a real problem into an algorithm shown as a flowchart or pseudo-code
successCriteria: All: decompose a problem into sub-problems
Most: draw a flowchart with a decision
Some: write pseudo-code for the same algorithm
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: order and precision in creation; excellence (itqan) in our work

keywords.def: breaking a problem into smaller parts
removing unnecessary detail
a precise set of steps to solve a problem
a structured, language-free way of writing an algorithm

hook.text: How would you explain to a robot how to make a cup of tea? What details could it ignore?
hook.a: Break it into steps (decomposition) and leave out details that do not matter, like the colour of the cup (abstraction).

islamicLink.text: Allah says He created death and life 'to test you as to which of you is best in deed' (Al-Mulk 67:2). Doing work with care and excellence (itqan), like careful, tested code, is part of being best in deed.

starter.a: a set of steps to solve a problem
options: a set of steps to solve a problem

starter.q: Which flowchart shape is a decision?

starter.a: e.g. a recipe, directions to school, wudu steps.

teach.heading: Decomposition and abstraction
bullets: Decomposition: break a problem into smaller parts
teach.note: Spec 1.1.1. Example: a school library app: search, borrow, return, overdue reminder.

teach.heading: Model: pass or fail
teach.note: Pupils draw the flowchart from this pseudo-code.

code.text:
SEND 'Enter mark' TO DISPLAY
RECEIVE mark FROM KEYBOARD
IF mark >= 50 THEN
    SEND 'Pass' TO DISPLAY
ELSE
    SEND 'Fail' TO DISPLAY
END IF

misconception.wrong: Abstraction means making the problem harder to understand
misconception.right: Abstraction hides detail that is not needed, so the problem is simpler

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share results; explain the right answer and the trap in the others.

check.q: Ignoring the colour of a bus when planning a bus-timetable app is ...
check.why: Removing unneeded detail is abstraction.

practice.q: Decompose a 'prayer-times reminder' app into four sub-problems.
practice.a: e.g. get location; get today's prayer times; compare with the current time; send a reminder.
practice.model: I do: 1) get the user's town; 2) look up today's five prayer times; 3) check the clock every minute; 4) when a time arrives, show a reminder.

practice.q: Which is a process box?

independent.q: Pupil PDF: draw a flowchart and write pseudo-code that inputs an age and outputs 'Child', 'Teen' (13 to 19) or 'Adult'.
independent.a: Two decisions: IF age < 13 → Child; ELSE IF age <= 19 → Teen; ELSE Adult.
independent.model: The teacher draws the first decision: diamond 'age < 13?', yes → output 'Child'.

independent.q: Extend: identify one abstraction you made.
independent.a: e.g. ignored date of birth; used whole years only.

independent.q: Stretch: how many test values would you use, and which?
independent.a: 12, 13, 19, 20 (boundaries) and an invalid value like -1.

exit.q: Breaking a problem into smaller parts is ...
exit.a: decomposition

keywords.def: instructions carried out one after another in order

starter: Bismillah. What does a diamond mean in a flowchart?

teach.heading: Three constructs
bullets: Sequence: step after step, in order
Selection: if / elif / else chooses a path
Repetition: a loop runs steps again
teach.note: Every algorithm in the course, from bubble sort to a login check, is made from these. Show each as a flowchart shape: a straight line, a diamond with two exits, a diamond with a line looping back. Point out that each block has one entry and one exit.

teach.heading: Two kinds of repetition
bullets: Count-controlled: repeat a set number of times
Condition-controlled: repeat until a test is met
Choose for when the count is known, while when it is not
teach.note: Run both programs. The for loop knows it will run 4 times; the while loop stops when the total reaches 10 or more, and that depends on the values. Ask pupils what happens if the condition never becomes false: an infinite loop.

code.text:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total = total + n
print(total)

stock = 20
weeks = 0
while stock > 0:
    stock = stock - 6
    weeks = weeks + 1
print(weeks)

teach.heading: Iteration over a data structure
bullets: Visit every item of a list in turn
Selection inside the loop filters items
Variables such as count store the result
teach.note: The loop variable takes each value of the list in turn; there is no index to manage. Point out that the if is inside the loop because it must be asked about every item. Pupils often put count = 0 inside the loop; show why that resets it each time.

teach.heading: Worked example: highest mark
teach.note: Model the thinking: set the first item as the highest so far, then compare each other item. Check with the trace: 45 -> 72 -> 72 -> 72 -> 90. Ask pupils why we do not start the highest at 0 (it fails for negative data, and starting with an item in the list is safer).

model.problem: Write pseudocode that outputs the highest value in the list temps = [14, 19, 11, 22, 17].
steps: Set highest to the first item, temps[0] (14)
FOR each t IN temps: compare t with highest
IF t > highest THEN set highest to t
After the loop ends, OUTPUT highest
model.answer: highest = 14, 19, 19, 22, 22, so the output is 22. It uses sequence, iteration over the list and selection inside it.

teach.heading: Check: which construct?
teach.note: Answer B. A is selection, C sequence, D a count-controlled loop. Ask pupils to say what the output is when the loop has run (the running total each time). A common slip is to call any loop 'selection' because it has a condition.

check.q: An algorithm asks for passwords until the user types the correct one. Which construct repeats the question?
check.why: The number of attempts is unknown in advance, so the loop is controlled by a condition. A count-controlled loop (D) needs a known number of repeats; selection (C) chooses but does not repeat.

lessons.title: Efficiency of searches and sorts
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we decide which algorithm is better when they all give the right answer?
objectives: Explain how bubble sort, merge sort, linear search and binary search work (1.2.6)
Compare algorithms by counting passes and comparisons (1.2.7)
Choose a suitable algorithm for a given situation
successCriteria: All: describe each algorithm in one sentence
Most: carry out a merge sort and count binary search checks
Some: justify an algorithm choice by comparing the number of comparisons as the list grows
lessons.smsc: Moral: ihsan (excellence) in choosing the best method, not just the first one

keywords.def: how little time or memory an algorithm needs for a job
checking two values against each other
one complete run through the list in a sort
arranged in a given order, such as ascending

starter: Bismillah. Why must a list be sorted before a binary search?
Sort 4, 9, 2 using bubble sort and show the list after the first pass.
Write the middle item of 2, 5, 8, 11, 14.

teach.heading: Bubble sort in code
bullets: Compare neighbours, swap if out of order
Repeat passes until a pass has no swaps
Output shows the list after each pass
teach.note: Pupils have met bubble sort in lesson 5 of the existing unit; here we trace the code and count passes. Point out the swapped flag: it lets the algorithm stop early. Ask how many passes an already sorted list needs (one, to confirm no swaps).

code.text:
data = [5, 3, 8, 1]
passes = 0
swapped = True
while swapped:
    swapped = False
    for i in range(len(data) - 1):
        if data[i] > data[i + 1]:
            data[i], data[i + 1] = data[i + 1], data[i]
            swapped = True
    passes = passes + 1
    print(passes, data)

teach.heading: Binary search in code
bullets: Check the middle item each time
Discard half the list after every check
Count the checks to compare efficiency
teach.note: Trace the code with the whole class, drawing low, mid and high. The list is sorted, which is essential. Compare: a linear search would take 6 checks to reach 27, binary took fewer. Pupils should state the result in words using 'checks'.

code.text:
nums = [3, 8, 12, 15, 21, 27, 34, 40, 52]
target = 27
low = 0
high = len(nums) - 1
checks = 0
while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    checks = checks + 1
    if nums[mid] == target:
        print("found at", mid, "after", checks, "checks")
        break
    elif nums[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1

teach.heading: How the work grows
bullets: Linear search: up to n checks
Binary search: halves each time, about log2 n
Merge sort splits then merges; bubble sort needs many passes
teach.note: Let pupils notice that doubling the list adds only one extra check for binary search. This is the key idea for 'efficiency' answers. Merge sort needs extra memory for the merged lists; bubble sort sorts in place. Do not ask for formulae beyond this table.

teach.heading: Worked example: merge sort
teach.note: Model on the board in two colours: splits in one, merges in another. Emphasise that in the merge step the first items of each list are compared and the smaller is moved. Say the stages aloud: split, split, merge, merge. Link to the cost: the extra lists use more memory.

model.problem: Use a merge sort on 7, 2, 9, 4. Show every stage.
steps: Merge the two lists: compare 2 and 4 (take 2), 7 and 4 (take 4), 7 and 9 (take 7), then 9

teach.heading: Check: choosing an algorithm
teach.note: Answer B. The list is unsorted, so binary search would give wrong results (D, the trap). Sorting first just to search once is slow for a single lookup. Ask why the answer would change if the contacts list was searched thousands of times.

check.q: A teacher has an unsorted list of 40 names and wants to find one name once. Which is the best choice?
options: Binary search on the list as it is
check.why: With one search on an unsorted list, a linear search needs at most 40 checks and no sorting. Binary search only works on a sorted list (D), and sorting first (A, C) costs extra work for a single lookup.

teach.heading: Same thing in Python
bullets: and, or, not work on them
teach.note: Run the program: the output columns mirror the table (with True and False instead of 1 and 0). Ask pupils to match each column to the table. This shows that a truth table is just a record of every possible input.

False True False True True
True False False True False
True True True True False

teach.heading: Worked example: a combined expression
teach.note: Model by working out the middle column first: the bracket is evaluated before the final operator. Build the table row by row. Emphasise writing the intermediate column; marks are often given for it.

model.problem: Complete the truth table for the expression A OR (NOT B).
steps: Four rows for the inputs A and B: 00, 01, 10, 11
Combine with A using OR: row 00 -> 0 OR 1 = 1; row 01 -> 0 OR 0 = 0

teach.heading: Misconception: NOT over brackets
bullets: NOT A AND NOT B gives 1, 0, 0, 0
teach.note: Ask pupils to build both columns to prove it. The brackets matter: NOT applies to the whole bracket. This is useful when writing conditions such as not (a and b).

misconception.wrong: NOT (A AND B) is the same as (NOT A) AND (NOT B).
misconception.right: They are different. NOT (A AND B) is 1 unless both inputs are 1; (NOT A) AND (NOT B) is 1 only when both are 0.

teach.heading: Check: AND or OR?
teach.note: Answer D. 'Either' here means at least one, which is OR; then the output is 1 for rows with a 1 in A or B. Option A is the AND column. Ask how the table would change if the rule were: A AND NOT B.

check.q: A garden light switches on if the sensor detects movement (A) or the manual switch is on (B). For A = 1 and B = 0, what is the output?
check.why: The rule is OR, so one input at 1 is enough. The AND rule would give 0 (A, B). NOT A is not part of the rule (C).

teach.heading: Writing a CSV file
bullets: Open with 'w' to write (replaces the old file)
Each record is one line; fields are separated by commas

file = open("scores.csv", "r")
for line in file:
    name, score = line.strip().split(",")
    print(name, int(score) + 5)

split(',') makes a list of fields
Fields are strings: cast the numbers

teach.heading: What % and // are used for
bullets: Digits: n % 10 is the last digit
Time: // for whole units, % for the rest
teach.note: Model the time example below as a worked problem. Add: use % for 'every third' loops and for wrapping around (clock, days of week). Ask pupils to find the last digit of 4827 (7) and the number without it (482).

code.text:
seconds = 4000
hours = seconds // 3600
rest = seconds % 3600
minutes = rest // 60
secs = rest % 60
print(hours, minutes, secs)
print(4827 % 10, 4827 // 10)

teach.heading: Worked example: even and odd with %
teach.note: Model the idea: a remainder of 0 when dividing by 2 means even. The program is the heart of many Paper 2 tasks. Then add the relational and logical operators: and, or, not combine conditions. Note that and is worked out before or.

model.problem: Write a condition that is True when n is even and greater than 10, and trace it for n = 14 and n = 8.

n = 8: 8 % 2 = 0 (True) but 8 > 10 is False, so False
model.answer: The condition is n % 2 == 0 and n > 10. It is True for 14 and False for 8.

teach.heading: Misconception: and before or
bullets: and is worked out before or
True or False and False is True
Use brackets to show what you mean
teach.note: Run this in Python: print(True or False and False) gives True, because False and False is False and then True or False is True. With brackets (True or False) and False the answer is False. Brackets save marks.

misconception.wrong: True or False and False is False, because it is worked out left to right.
misconception.right: and is worked out first: False and False is False, then True or False is True. Brackets, (True or False) and False, would give False.

teach.heading: Check: evaluate
teach.note: Answer A. 3 ** 2 is 9, then 9 * 2 is 18, then plus 2 is 20. B ignores precedence (2 + 3) ** 2 * 2. C and D confuse ** with * or evaluate left to right.

check.q: What is the value of 2 + 3 ** 2 * 2 in Python?
check.why: ** is first: 3 ** 2 = 9, then 9 * 2 = 18, then 2 + 18 = 20. 50 comes from adding first, (2 + 3) ** 2 * 2 (B); 18 forgets to add the 2 (D).
